title: Using Props and Visual Hooks for Viral Videos
summary: Adley Kinsman explains how to use physical props and visual signage to hook social media viewers immediately. Instead of talking-head explanations, creators should start directly in the action with clear visual context that even a sixth grader can instantly understand.
key_points: Viewers cannot feel weight or effort through a screen, so physical attributes (like a 25-pound mug) must be clearly demonstrated visually rather than acted out.
Do not open a video by explaining the premise, stakes, or consequences; jump immediately into the action.
Provide context using a simple text overlay or a physical sign attached to the scene (e.g., writing '25 lb MUG' on poster board taped to the table) to act as a pseudo text overlay.
Rules of any challenge or game must be simple enough for a sixth grader to understand.
Pair a visual hook (such as an opening cut of someone physically shaking from the strain) before cutting back to the start.
Pay attention to visual contrast and pop of color (such as using red ink instead of black against outdoor green grass and blue sky).
Social media audiences scroll for entertainment, not business pitches; wrap real estate deals or coaching programs inside an entertaining visual container.

Transcript:
Adley Kinsman: "So that's a 25-pound coffee mug."
Speaker 2: "Oh, it's fucking heavy."
Adley Kinsman: "It's heavy, and no way you could actually drink out of it, right?"
Speaker 2: "No."
Adley Kinsman: "So if we're going to make a video out of this, the viewer can't tell. They don't know if this is 50 pounds, they don't know if this is 5 pounds, because we could always be acting. But they don't know if you're weak, they don't know if you're strong. So without having to start the video saying, 'Here's a 25-pound coffee mug, and let's see if you can do it, and here's the stakes and the consequences of if you can't'—we don't care. We want to start right in the action. So either want a text overlay that just explains the rules of the game—hint, the rules have to be simple enough a sixth grader could understand it..."
Speaker 2: "Are you listening to this, Alexa?"
Adley Kinsman: "...so even better than that, can we add a visual hook on top of somebody shaking in an opening shot, then cutting back to them starting? Can we demonstrate '25 pound'? And I wish I would have used red for 25 pounds, for the contrast, just for a pop of color, even though we're on green, it's bright..."
Speaker 2: "Wow."
Adley Kinsman: "...we're going to get the blue sky."
Speaker 2: "Little things."
Adley Kinsman: "It's all the little things. The nuance is the difference between good and great. And most people will just do a video, they won't think about the visuals, they won't think about the relationship to the text hook and the way the audience is pre-framed. But we have to think: they just watched a cat video, and now they're coming across our video. Do they want to learn about your real estate deal or your coaching program? No, they're on social media to be entertained. So we can design an entertaining container that compels them to watch something they wouldn't normally watch."
Speaker 2: "Master fucking class."
Adley Kinsman: "It's all these little subconscious things. But if we can think about them when we're designing our video, it makes it a lot easier to be successful every single time. And then we'll tape this here, and then probably have people film on the corner so this is present every time as pseudo text overlay. But now, when people are shaking, we immediately have context and we don't have to talking-head explain ourselves. We can start right in the action with the high stakes."
